near_miss.why_not: Irish explains an epithet by deaths of both parents; Homer asks the name given by parents or has Odysseus name Nobody. The parents are not the naming agents in Irish, and naming/kinship co-occurrence does not establish inherited syntax. Vedic corpus searches also locate ordinary parent pairings (RV 1.24.1–2; 1.89.4), without the Irish death/name nexus.

Serbian and Russian have a close Slavic parallel, but these are one branch. Irish priest bringing fish, wine and wheat and Norse mermaid description provide no cross-branch counterpart; cannot meet the anchoring rule.

Irish angelic promise concerns personal bodily survival until Judgment; Sanskrit epic concerns survival in fame, and Atharvaveda longevity with gold. No common collocation accompanies the life root, and Christian eschatology gives the Irish passage a specific later frame.

Irish nige is the verbal noun of nigid, but husci/husce denotes the river sides where the woman places her feet, not the instrument governed by washing. Homer treats wounds with warm water; Hesiod prescribes handwashing before river crossing. Corpus search found 10 washing/water units, including the parallel Irish recension G300011:#1/84:4 and G303000:#1:799, but no marked shared collocation is supplied by these slab anchors. Literal washing with water would in any event require more diagnostic wording.
